question: What is the main purpose of Lean?
options: Reduce waste and improve customer value
Increase output by adding more inspection staff
Add more approval steps to reduce risk in the process
Measure only employee satisfaction across departments
explanation: Lean improves customer value and flow by reducing non-value-adding work. (Syllabus Ch.1, p.3)

question: What is the main focus of Six Sigma?
options: Increasing inventory to buffer demand peaks
Adding process steps to check the quality
Producing more than needed to avoid stock-outs
Reducing defects and variation
explanation: Six Sigma reduces defects and undesirable variation through disciplined measurement and analysis. (Syllabus Ch.1, p.3)

question: What does Muda mean?
options: Unevenness
Waste
Overburden
Customer demand
explanation: Muda is waste: activity that consumes resources without adding value. (Syllabus Ch.1, p.3)

question: What does Mura mean?
options: Unevenness
Waste
Equipment maintenance
Error-proofing
explanation: Mura is unevenness or irregular demand/workload; Muri is overburdening people or equipment. (Syllabus Ch.1, p.3)

question: Which pair represents the two main pillars of the Toyota Production System?
options: Kaizen and Hoshin Kanri
SIPOC and the project charter
Just-in-Time and Jidoka
5S and SMED for quick changeovers
explanation: TPS is supported by Just-in-Time and Jidoka (build quality in and stop to address abnormalities). (Syllabus Ch.1, p.3)

question: What is Kaizen?
options: A one-time large investment in new equipment
Continuous incremental improvement
A way to calculate the defects per million
A type of final inspection done by the quality team
explanation: Kaizen is continuous, incremental improvement involving the people doing the work. (Syllabus Ch.1, p.3)

question: Which activity is an example of waiting waste?
options: An employee corrects an error made earlier in the process
A team enters the same data twice in two systems
A worker walks to a distant printer to collect a document
A ticket stays in a queue for two days
explanation: Waiting is idle time; a ticket sitting in a queue for two days is the typical example. (Syllabus Ch.2, p.4)

question: What does the S in SIPOC stand for?
options: Systems
Suppliers
Solutions
Standards
explanation: SIPOC = Suppliers, Inputs, Process, Outputs, Customers. (Syllabus Ch.4, p.5)

question: What does VOC stand for?
options: Value of Capacity
Variation of Control
Verification of Costs
Voice of the Customer
explanation: Voice of the Customer: evidence of customers' needs, expectations and experiences. (Syllabus Ch.4, p.5)

question: Which DMAIC phase comes first?
options: Measure
Improve
Define
Control
explanation: DMAIC = Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control. (Syllabus Ch.3, p.5)

question: Which DMAIC phase aims to sustain improvements?
options: Control
Analyze
Define
Measure
explanation: Control sustains the gains: owners, monitoring and reaction rules. (Syllabus Ch.3 p.5 and Ch.13 p.12)

question: What is a typical Green Belt responsibility?
options: Leading a defined process-improvement project
Approving all company budgets for improvement work
Replacing the project sponsor when a project is delayed
Managing only the repairs of the production equipment
explanation: A Green Belt leads bounded improvement projects, commonly alongside normal duties. (Syllabus Ch.3, p.4)

question: What is the main purpose of a swimlane diagram?
options: Calculate the availability of the equipment per shift
Set product prices based on the cost of each step
Show process activities by role or department
Measure the number of defect opportunities per unit
explanation: A swimlane diagram assigns activities to actors, departments or systems and exposes handoffs. (Syllabus Ch.5, p.6)

question: What does takt time describe?
options: The required pace to meet customer demand
The total waiting time of one customer in the queue
The number of defects found per unit produced
The time that a team needs for its daily meeting
explanation: Takt time = net available time ÷ customer demand: the required pace, not an observed time. (Syllabus Ch.6, p.7)

question: A team has 400 available minutes and demand for 100 requests. What is the takt time?
options: 2 minutes per request
10 minutes per request
40 minutes per request
4 minutes per request
explanation: 400 ÷ 100 = 4 minutes per request. (Syllabus Ch.6, p.7)

question: What does First Time Right (FTR) measure?
options: Total inventory held in storage at the end of the month
Number of employees working on each shift in the plant at night
Work completed correctly without rework on the first attempt
Time spent waiting for approval from the manager each week
explanation: FTR = units completed correctly without rework on the first attempt ÷ units processed × 100%. (Syllabus Ch.6, p.7)

question: What is the purpose of the 5 Whys method?
options: Determine the salaries of the employees in a team
Calculate the daily demand for each product line
Explore possible underlying causes of a problem
Schedule the maintenance of the machines each week
explanation: 5 Whys repeatedly asks why a condition occurred to explore underlying causes. (Syllabus Ch.8, p.8)

question: What is a fishbone (Ishikawa) diagram used for?
options: Calculating takt time for the whole process
Organizing possible causes of a problem
Setting the financial budgets of the departments
Measuring the production output of each machine
explanation: A fishbone organizes possible causes (hypotheses) of a problem; it does not prove them. (Syllabus Ch.8, p.9)

question: Which sequence correctly lists the five 5S steps?
options: Scan, Schedule, Simplify, Standardize, Safeguard
Sort, Set in Order, Shine, Standardize, Sustain
Select, Store, Sweep, Standardize, Sustain
Start, Search, Streamline, Support, Safeguard
explanation: 5S = Sort, Set in Order, Shine, Standardize, Sustain. (Syllabus Ch.11, p.11)

question: What is OEE calculated from?
options: Lead time × Demand × Inventory level
Defects × Units × Opportunities per unit
Cost × Delivery speed × Staffing level
Availability × Performance × Quality
explanation: OEE = Availability × Performance × Quality. (Syllabus Ch.12, p.12)

question: What is the difference between Lean and Six Sigma?
modelAnswer: Lean emphasizes value, flow and waste reduction; Six Sigma emphasizes defects, variation and process capability.

question: Name the five Lean principles in order.
modelAnswer: Value, value stream, flow, pull, perfection.

question: Which two pillars are associated with TPS?
modelAnswer: Just-in-Time and Jidoka.

question: What are Muda, Mura and Muri?
modelAnswer: Waste, unevenness and overburden.

question: What is the difference between motion and transportation waste?
modelAnswer: Motion concerns unnecessary movement of people; transportation concerns movement of items, materials or information.

question: What is the eighth waste in the common eight-waste model?
modelAnswer: Unused employee talent or skills.
flag: The Lesson 3 slide "The 7 Wastes" shows only seven (no unused talent). The syllabus uses eight (TIMWOODS). Follow whichever your lecturer used in class.

question: What is a ninth sustainability waste lens?
modelAnswer: Avoidable environmental resource use, emissions or materials. It is not a universally standard ninth category.

question: What does SIPOC stand for?
modelAnswer: Suppliers, Inputs, Process, Outputs, Customers.

question: What is a Champion responsible for?
modelAnswer: Sponsoring and aligning improvement work, securing resources and removing barriers.
explanation: The Champion/Sponsor is a senior leader and a governance role, not a technical belt. (Syllabus Ch.3, p.4; Lesson 1 slide 10)

question: Which DMAIC phase typically contains the Project Charter?
explanation: The charter clarifies the problem, goal and scope, which is what Define does. (Syllabus Ch.3, p.5)

question: What does the "I" in DMAIC stand for?
explanation: Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control.

question: What is the final DMAIC phase?
explanation: Control sustains the gains.

question: What is a tollgate?
modelAnswer: A phase-end evidence review and authorization decision.
explanation: A sponsor checks the evidence and authorizes the next phase. It is not an extra DMAIC phase. (Syllabus Ch.3, p.5)

question: What is the role of a Green Belt?
modelAnswer: Leading bounded improvement projects and applying appropriate analytical methods.

question: What is the role of a White Belt?
modelAnswer: Basic awareness of Lean Six Sigma and support for the improvement culture.

question: Is the Master Black Belt a project sponsor?
modelAnswer: Not by definition. It is a technical coaching/deployment role, while the Champion is typically the sponsor.

question: What is Kaizen?
modelAnswer: Continuous incremental improvement with staff involvement.

question: What is a Poka Yoke example?
modelAnswer: A connector that fits only the correct orientation, or a form that rejects invalid input.
explanation: Poka Yoke = error-proofing: making errors difficult to create or easy to detect. (Syllabus Ch.10, p.11)

question: Must the 5 Whys method ask exactly five questions?
modelAnswer: No. Continue until the causes are sufficiently evidenced and actionable.
explanation: Five is a mnemonic, not a mandatory count. (Syllabus Ch.8, p.8)

question: What is an Ishikawa diagram also called?
explanation: Fishbone or cause-and-effect diagram.

question: What is root cause analysis for?
modelAnswer: To investigate and verify the mechanisms that produce a problem, not merely treat symptoms.

question: What is the difference between takt time and cycle time?
modelAnswer: Takt is the demand-based required pace; cycle time is the observed process cycle / output interval, depending on definition.

question: What is lead time?
modelAnswer: Elapsed time from request to delivery, including waiting.

question: Calculate takt time for 450 available minutes and demand of 150 (minutes per unit).
explanation: 450 / 150 = 3 minutes per unit.

question: What does DPMO stand for?
explanation: Note: it counts defects per million opportunities, not defective units per million.

question: Compute DPMO: 24 defects, 400 units, 3 opportunities each.
What is First Time Right?
modelAnswer: Completing work correctly without rework on the first attempt.

question: What is a swimlane diagram?
modelAnswer: A process map that assigns steps to roles, teams or systems and shows handoffs.

question: What is a Value Stream Map?
modelAnswer: A map of end-to-end work and information flows, time and inventory/queues.

question: What does 5S stand for?
modelAnswer: Sort, Set in Order, Shine, Standardize, Sustain.

question: What is Kanban?
modelAnswer: A visual pull/replenishment and work-in-progress control mechanism.

question: What is SMED?
modelAnswer: A systematic method to reduce changeover time by separating and simplifying internal and external activities.

question: What is TPM?
modelAnswer: Total Productive Maintenance.
explanation: It combines proactive maintenance, operator involvement, planned maintenance, quality maintenance and systematic loss reduction. (Syllabus Ch.12, p.12)

question: Calculate OEE: 0.9 × 0.8 × 0.95 (answer as a percentage).
What is Hoshin Kanri?
modelAnswer: Deployment and alignment of strategy with operational objectives and reviews.

question: What is the purpose of a control plan?
modelAnswer: To monitor and sustain the improvement with clear owners and response rules.

question: Is a fishbone diagram proof of root causes?
modelAnswer: No. It organizes hypotheses that need verification.

question: Which statement best separates Lean from Six Sigma?
options: Lean targets waste across the value stream; Six Sigma targets defects and variation
Lean focuses on statistical variation and capability; Six Sigma focuses on removing waste and flow
Lean applies only to manufacturing, while Six Sigma applies only to service and IT processes
They are rival approaches, so an organisation has to choose one and drop the other
explanation: Lean = value, flow and waste. Six Sigma = defects, variation and capability. Neither is limited to manufacturing, and they complement each other.

question: What does Jidoka mean in TPS?
options: Producing exactly what is needed, exactly when it is needed
Building quality in and stopping to fix abnormalities
Levelling production volume and mix to smooth the workload
A visual or audible signal that asks for support
explanation: Jidoka stops or signals an abnormal condition. Just-in-Time is the other pillar of TPS.

question: What does Heijunka do?
options: Stops the line when a defect appears
Coordinates production with demand
Levels production volume and mix
Signals that help is needed
explanation: Heijunka = leveling. It reduces peaks in volume and mix where demand and constraints permit.

question: What is an Andon?
options: A level production schedule for volume and mix
A system that produces only what the customer demands
A small-scale test of a change before roll-out
A visual or audible signal requesting support
explanation: Andon signals abnormal conditions so that help can be called.

question: An unstable schedule leads to overtime, errors and queues. Which chain of the 3Ms describes this?
options: Mura (unevenness) causes Muri (overburden), then Muda (waste)
Muda (waste) causes Mura (unevenness), which in turn removes Muri (overburden)
Muri (overburden) causes Kaizen, which then removes Mura (unevenness)
Muda, Mura and Muri are three separate problems that do not affect one another
explanation: The 3Ms reinforce one another: unstable schedules (Mura) can cause overtime (Muri), errors and queues (Muda).

question: In the PDCA cycle, what happens in the "Check / Study" step?
options: You plan the change and make a prediction
You compare the results with the prediction
You test the change on a small scale
You adopt, adapt or abandon the change
explanation: Plan: change + prediction. Do: small-scale test. Check/Study: compare results with prediction. Act: adopt, adapt or abandon and standardize.

question: Just-in-Time coordinates production with demand; it is more than merely keeping inventory low.
explanation: JIT coordinates production with demand. These methods require stable processes and must not be confused with merely reducing inventory.

question: What is the correct order of the five Lean principles?
options: Value, flow, value stream, perfection, pull
Flow, pull, value, perfection, value stream
Perfection, value, flow, pull, value stream
Value, value stream, flow, pull, perfection
explanation: Define value, map the value stream, create flow, let work be pulled by demand, pursue perfection.

question: An IT ticket is copied between three teams. Which waste is this?
options: Transportation
Motion
Overproduction
Inventory
explanation: Transportation = unnecessary movement of materials or information between places. Motion is unnecessary movement by a person.

question: An employee knows how to automate a task, but nobody ever asks them. Which waste is this?
options: Defects and rework
Skills / unused talent
Waiting and idle time
Overprocessing of tasks
explanation: Not using employee expertise and ideas is the eighth waste (the S in TIMWOODS).

question: A team enters the same data twice. Which waste is this?
options: Waiting
Defects
Overprocessing
Transportation
explanation: Overprocessing = more work than needed. The syllabus lists "entered twice" as its example.

question: What describes a Gemba (waste) walk?
options: An inspection round to find out who is at fault for the errors
A review of dashboards and status reports in the meeting room
A statistical audit of defect data collected over the past year
Observing at the real workplace, without blame, and recording facts
explanation: Gemba is learning at the real workplace, not an inspection to find fault. Distinguish observation from interpretation.

question: Environmental waste is one of the universally standardized eight wastes.
explanation: It is sometimes added as a ninth sustainability lens, but it is not one of the standardized eight.

question: Compared with the classic seven wastes, which waste does the eight-waste model (TIMWOODS) add?
options: Overproduction (too much, too early)
Skills / unused talent
Waiting (idle time)
Transportation (moving items)
explanation: The slide "The 7 Wastes" shows overproduction, inventory, transportation, motion, waiting, defects and overprocessing. The syllabus adds unused talent.
flag: Slide shows 7 wastes, the syllabus 8. Check which version your lecturer expects.

question: What does a strict value-added test ask about an activity?
options: Does it keep staff busy and make full use of their available working hours throughout the day?
Is it required by the department that performs it and written in its procedures?
Does it transform the product, is it done right first time and valued by the customer?
Was it cheap to perform compared with the same activity elsewhere in the company?
explanation: Some non-value-added work is currently necessary for legal or risk reasons; classify it separately from removable waste.

question: Which description fits the Champion / Sponsor?
options: Someone who leads bounded improvement projects alongside normal duties
A methodological expert who coaches Green Belts and supports deployment
Someone who takes part in improvement activities and data collection
A senior leader who selects projects, secures resources and removes barriers
explanation: The Champion is a governance role, not a technical belt. The first option describes a Green Belt, the second a Master Black Belt, the third a Yellow Belt.

question: Which belt leads complex analytical projects and coaches Green Belts?
options: Black Belt
Yellow Belt
White Belt
Champion
explanation: Black Belt: leads complex analytical projects and coaches Green Belts. Master Black Belt: methodological expert and deployment coach.

question: What is a tollgate?
options: An additional sixth phase that follows Control
A formal review where a sponsor authorizes the next phase
A statistical test used to check the quality of the data
A kick-off meeting of the whole project team
explanation: A tollgate is not an additional DMAIC phase.

question: A tollgate is a formal review at which a sponsor authorizes the next DMAIC phase.
explanation: DMAIC has five phases. A tollgate is the formal review at the end of a phase, not an extra phase.

question: What should the problem statement in a project charter avoid?
options: Describing the process boundaries
Stating the business case
Listing the stakeholders
Specifying a preferred solution
explanation: A charter has business case and VOB, problem statement, goal, scope, boundaries, stakeholders, team, timeline, assumptions and risks. Avoid pre-selecting the solution.

question: What does SMART stand for in a SMART goal?
options: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound
Simple, Measured, Approved, Reviewed, Tested
Specific, Managed, Accountable, Realistic, Timely
Strategic, Measurable, Agreed, Reported, Tracked
explanation: SMART goals are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound.

question: In a RACI chart, how many Accountable owners should a decision normally have?
options: Two
One
As many as there are Consulted people
None
explanation: RACI = Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed. Normally only one accountable owner per decision.

question: Which is the strongest charter goal?
options: Improve our international-student app by implementing AI as soon as possible
Make the helpdesk better for students so that they are more satisfied
Cut the median onboarding resolution time from 72 to 36 hours by 30 June
Install a new ticketing tool at the helpdesk before the end of this year
explanation: A strong goal is specific and measurable with a baseline, target and deadline, and does not prescribe the solution. The syllabus's version also protects first-contact resolution. "Implement AI" is the syllabus's weak-charter example.

question: Belt definitions and prerequisites are identical across all certifying bodies.
explanation: They vary among certifying bodies.

question: What does VOB (Voice of the Business) cover?
options: Strategic, financial, regulatory and operational priorities
Evidence from customer interviews, surveys and complaints
Statistical limits that describe how a process behaves
Employee satisfaction scores and staff turnover figures
explanation: VOC is the customers' needs and experiences. VOB covers the organization's own priorities.

question: Which is a well-formed CTQ?
options: Support should be fast, friendly and easy to reach for students at any time
90% of priority-2 tickets get a first response within 4 business hours
Customers must be happy with the service they receive from us
The helpdesk team should work harder to answer incoming requests
explanation: A CTQ turns a broad need into an observable requirement with an operational definition, target, unit, measurement method and owner.

question: Roughly how many high-level steps should the P (Process) of a SIPOC have?
options: 1 or 2
4 to 7
As many as the detailed map has
explanation: SIPOC defines boundaries and interfaces. It is not a detailed process map.

question: A SIPOC is a high-level summary of a process, not a detailed process map.
explanation: It summarizes suppliers, inputs, process, outputs and customers, and defines boundaries and interfaces.

question: Complete the acronym: Suppliers, Inputs, ____, Outputs, Customers.
explanation: SIPOC = Suppliers, Inputs, Process, Outputs, Customers.

question: In the coffee-service SIPOC, which is an output?
options: Coffee beans, water, milk and biscuits
A served beverage and the transaction
The coffee, milk and bakery suppliers
The guest placing an order at the counter
explanation: Suppliers: coffee, milk, bakery and guest. Inputs: beans, water, milk, biscuit, order. Outputs: beverage and transaction. Customers: guest and business owner.

question: In a SIPOC diagram of a pizza process, which entries are in the Customers column?
options: Dairy Supply Corporation and Vegetable Farmers United
Cheese, olives, peppers, dough and sauce
Dine-in, take-out and delivery customers
Prepare dough, add sauce, bake in oven
explanation: The other options are the Suppliers, the Inputs and the Process column.
flag: Image slide: read from the slide picture.

question: What do cross-lane transfers in a swimlane diagram reveal?
options: How satisfied the customer is with the result
The number of defects per million opportunities
How well the equipment is being utilized
Handoffs, ownership gaps and repeated approvals
explanation: A swimlane assigns activities to actors, departments or systems.

question: Which data does a value stream map often include?
options: Cycle times, changeover times and lead time
Employee salaries, bonuses and overtime hours
Customer satisfaction scores per department
Organization charts and reporting lines
explanation: VSM shows material and information flows, with current-state and future-state maps built from measured data.

question: A request needs 18 minutes of value-added work but spends 3 calendar days (4,320 minutes) in total. What is the PCE in percent (2 decimals)?
explanation: PCE = value-added time / lead time × 100% = 18 / 4,320 × 100 = 0.42%.

question: What is a future-state map?
options: A guaranteed result of the improvement
The same as the current-state map
A hypothesis until it has been tested
A list of all the wastes found
explanation: Map the current state before designing the future state.

question: It is fine to mix minutes of staff effort with calendar days of customer lead time in one PCE calculation.
explanation: This is a listed mapping pitfall. Use consistent units and state whether non-working hours are included.

question: Available time is 420 minutes per day and demand is 140 units per day. What is the takt time (minutes per unit)?
explanation: Takt = 420 / 140 = 3 minutes per unit.

question: A station needs 4 minutes per unit, but the takt time is 3 minutes per unit. What follows?
options: The station is faster than needed, so it will often stand idle
The station cannot meet demand without redesign or parallel capacity
Demand will fall until it matches the capacity of the station
Nothing happens, because takt time is only an average figure
explanation: Takt is the required pace; a cycle time above takt means the station is too slow.

question: There are 80 open cases and 20 cases are completed per day. By Little's Law, what is the average flow time in days?
explanation: Flow time = WIP / throughput = 80 / 20 = 4 days.

question: Which formula is Little's Law?
options: Average WIP = customer demand ÷ station cycle time
Throughput rate = average lead time × WIP
Average flow time = takt time × WIP
Average WIP = throughput rate × average flow time
explanation: For a stable system with consistent averages. It is an average relationship, not a guarantee for individual cases.

question: Little's Law describes an average relationship for a stable system, not a guarantee for individual cases.
explanation: Average WIP = throughput rate × average flow time, for a stable system with consistent averages.

question: Takt time is the observed processing time of a station.
explanation: Takt is the required rhythm to match demand; the observed time is the cycle time.

question: There are 60 open requests and 30 are completed per day. What is the average flow time in days?
explanation: 60 / 30 = 2 days (Little's Law).

question: What is the bottleneck of a process?
options: The step that costs the most money to run each day
The step where the largest number of employees work
The first step in the flow, where the work enters
The step that limits the output of the whole process
explanation: Capacity is the maximum sustainable output; the bottleneck limits it, so improvements elsewhere may not increase end-to-end throughput.

question: 500 forms are processed and 40 defects are found. What is the DPU (defects per unit)?
explanation: DPU = total defects / total units = 40 / 500 = 0.08.

question: 500 forms with 4 predefined opportunities each, and 40 defects. What is the DPO?
500 forms with 4 opportunities each and 40 defects. What is the DPMO?
In 500 forms, 40 defects are spread over 35 forms. What is the defective-unit rate?
explanation: 35 / 500 = 7%. The 8% figure (40 / 500) is the DPU, which counts defects, not defective units.

question: DPMO measures defects per million opportunities, not defective units per million.
How is rolled throughput yield (RTY) calculated?
options: As the average of the first-pass yields of all the steps
As the product of the step first-pass yields
From the final inspection result only
As the sum of defects divided by units
explanation: Do not infer RTY from final inspection alone.

question: The common benchmark of about 3.4 DPMO for Six Sigma rests on what?
options: A legal standard set by regulators
A short-term measurement on one machine
A long-term 1.5-sigma shift convention
The number of steps in the process
explanation: It is a convention, not a universal physical law. Report actual DPMO and assumptions rather than sigma labels alone.

question: Compute the DPMO for 1,200 units with 3 opportunities each and 54 defects.
explanation: 54 / (1,200 × 3) × 1,000,000 = 15,000. It does not follow that 54 units are defective.

question: What should the number of defect opportunities per unit reflect?
options: Meaningful CTQs, not an inflated count
As many different checks as possible
The number of employees who touch the unit
The number of steps in the process map
explanation: A defect opportunity is a specified chance for one defect to occur per unit. Do not inflate the count to make performance look better.

question: Which are the typical 6M categories of a fishbone diagram?
options: Money, Marketing, Management, Machine, Market, Motivation
People, Machine, Method, Material, Measurement, Environment
Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control, Maintenance
Suppliers, Inputs, Process, Outputs, Customers, Management
explanation: Syllabus wording: Manpower/People, Machine, Method, Material, Measurement, Mother Nature/Environment. Adapt the categories to services (e.g. people, process, technology, culture, procedure, environment, as in the Lesson 2 hotel exercise).

question: In an Ishikawa diagram, which part represents the problem or defect?
options: The long backbone of the diagram
The ribs branching off the backbone
The head of the fish
The tail at the left end
explanation: The defect is the fish's head, facing right. Causes extend to the left as fishbones, with ribs for major causes and sub-branches for root causes.

question: What is true about the 80/20 rule in a Pareto analysis?
options: It always holds exactly
It only applies to defects, never to cost
It means 20% of causes are always cheap to fix
It is a heuristic, not a guaranteed distribution
explanation: Prioritize on impact and feasibility, not frequency alone.

question: What is an A3?
options: A one-page narrative from background and analysis to follow-up
A control chart used for monitoring the proportion of defective items
A kind of Kanban card that signals the replenishment of materials
A scoring method that ranks failure modes by severity and occurrence
explanation: A concise one-page narrative of background, current condition, target, analysis, countermeasures, implementation and follow-up. It encourages evidence, shared thinking and coaching.

question: How is the traditional FMEA risk priority number (RPN) calculated?
options: Severity + Occurrence + Detectability
Severity × Occurrence × Detectability
Defects × Units × Opportunities
Cost × Speed × Staffing
explanation: RPN is a prioritization aid with known limitations.

question: A failure mode with a modest RPN can be ignored even when its severity is high.
explanation: High-severity risks deserve attention even when the RPN is modest.

question: When is a "root cause" useful?
options: When it names the person who is responsible for the failure
When it is the fifth answer in a series of why questions
When it is the most frequently reported symptom
When it is actionable and explains why the problem recurs
explanation: Verify whether changing the cause changes the outcome before calling it a root cause.

question: Lead times are often right-skewed. Which statistics are then useful?
options: Median and P90
Only the mean
Only the range
Only the sample size
explanation: Also show sample size, time window and missing values.

question: Control limits on a control chart are statistically derived from process data; they are not the customer's specification limits.
explanation: Control limits are statistically derived from process data and are not specification limits.

question: Which control chart suits the weekly proportion of defective forms?
options: I-MR chart
X-bar/R chart
p-chart
u-chart
explanation: I-MR: individual continuous values. X-bar/R: rational subgroups. p-chart: proportion defective. u-chart: defects per unit with varying exposure.

question: A process that looks capable by Cp/Cpk is reliably predictable even if it is unstable.
explanation: Assess stability first. A capable-looking unstable process is not reliably predictable.

question: What are special-cause variations?
options: Identifiable, unusual influences
Variation arising from the current system itself
Variation inside the specification limits
Variation in customer demand only
explanation: Common causes arise from the current system; special causes are identifiable unusual influences.

question: What are benefits of one-piece (continuous) flow?
options: It increases batch sizes so work moves in bigger groups
It reduces WIP and makes defects visible quickly
It removes the need for reliable steps and balanced workloads
It lowers customer demand by shortening the delivery time
explanation: It requires suitable workload balance, reliable steps and sensible exceptions.

question: What characterizes a pull system?
options: Work is pushed forward in large batches from upstream steps
Work goes to whichever queue happens to be the longest
Downstream consumption authorizes new work or replenishment
Managers decide and assign all of the work in advance
explanation: Kanban is a typical tool for pull.

question: What does Kanban do?
options: It calculates defects per million opportunities
It levels demand by changing prices during peak weeks
It stops the line when a defect is detected
It visualizes work and limits work in progress
explanation: Explicit WIP limits help prevent overloading and expose blocked work.

question: Which is an example of Poka Yoke?
options: A required-format field that rejects invalid input
A weekly status meeting about the open tickets
An extra approval step after an error occurred
A poster that reminds staff to be careful with data
explanation: Poka Yoke = error-proofing: keyed connectors, required-format fields, barcode validation.

question: With Jidoka, detecting an abnormality must trigger a response.
explanation: Detection without reaction is insufficient. Jidoka stops or alerts on abnormality and triggers a response.

question: For line balancing you compare the cycle time of each step with the ____ time.
explanation: Compare step cycle times with takt, then redistribute work at the constraint.

question: A team limits "In Progress" to eight tickets and adds mandatory category validation. Which tools does this combine?
options: SMED and 5S
Heijunka and Hoshin Kanri
FMEA and Pareto
Kanban and Poka Yoke
explanation: WIP limit = Kanban. Mandatory validation = Poka Yoke (error-proofing).

question: What does the first S of 5S, Sort, mean?
options: Remove unnecessary items
Locate and label needed items
Clean and inspect
Agree visual standards
explanation: Set in Order: locate and label. Shine: clean and inspect. Standardize: agree standards and routines. Sustain: audit and coach.

question: What does "Standardize" mean in 5S?
options: Remove unnecessary items from the area
Agree visual standards and routines
Audit, coach and improve habits
Clean and inspect the work area
explanation: Sustain is the S that audits and coaches habits.

question: Some organizations add Safety as a sixth S.
explanation: Stated in the syllabus.

question: In SMED, what are "external" activities?
options: Activities that are carried out by suppliers outside the company
Activities that need the equipment to be shut down first
Activities that are removed from the changeover completely
Activities that can be done while the equipment runs
explanation: Internal activities require shutdown. Convert, simplify, parallelize and standardize.

question: What is the relation between standardized work and Kaizen?
options: Standardization enables Kaizen instead of freezing improvement
Standards are fixed once agreed and must not be changed by staff
Kaizen replaces the need for any standard way of working
Only managers are allowed to design and revise the standards
explanation: Employees should help design and revise the standard.

question: Visual management should make normal and abnormal conditions obvious and trigger action.
explanation: A dashboard that no one acts on is not effective visual management.

question: What should happen when a daily stand-up uncovers a complex problem?
options: Solve it right away during the stand-up itself
Ignore it until the next monthly review meeting
Escalate it to a separate problem-solving session
Replace the stand-up with a status report
explanation: The stand-up should not become a long status meeting.

question: Planned time 480 min, downtime 60 min, ideal cycle 2 min, total output 180, good output 171. What is the OEE in percent?
Operating time 420 min, ideal cycle time 2 min, total count 180. What is the Performance in percent (1 decimal)?
explanation: Performance = (ideal cycle time × total count) / operating time = 360 / 420 = 85.7%.

question: Which of these is NOT one of the six big losses?
options: Breakdowns of equipment
A drop in sales volume
Reduced speed of the machine
Minor stops and short idling
explanation: The six: breakdowns, setup/adjustments, minor stops, reduced speed, startup rejects and production rejects.

question: What does Total Productive Maintenance (TPM) combine?
options: Only specialist repairs carried out after a machine breaks down
Only basic cleaning and inspection done by the operators
Planned maintenance, operator involvement and loss reduction
Replacement of all equipment on a fixed yearly schedule
explanation: TPM combines proactive maintenance, operator involvement, planned maintenance, quality maintenance and systematic loss reduction. Operators may do safe basic care; specialist maintenance and safety obligations remain.

question: In the Theory of Constraints, what follows right after identifying the system constraint?
options: Reduce all other steps
Remove the constraint step from the process
Add inventory in front of every step
Exploit and protect it
explanation: Identify, exploit and protect, subordinate other steps, elevate capacity where justified, then reassess.

question: Which item belongs in a control plan?
options: A reaction threshold with an escalation path
The price list of the main supplier of materials
The list of all customer names and addresses
The full process map of the old process
explanation: A control plan also holds the CTQ/KPI, operational definition, target, data source, frequency, process owner, display, reaction threshold, corrective action and escalation path.

question: What is catchball in Hoshin Kanri?
options: A way to rank defects by their frequency, cost and severity
A dialogue to align goals with feasibility across levels
A meeting format used for the short daily huddles
A method to count the steps of a process map
explanation: Catchball is a dialogue to align ambition, resources and practical feasibility across levels. Hoshin Kanri translates strategic priorities into breakthrough goals, annual objectives, owners and review cycles.

question: How do DMAIC and PDCA relate?
options: They are competing methods, so you should use only one of them
PDCA is the project version of DMAIC; DMAIC is for daily use
DMAIC is a project path; PDCA is a repeating learning cycle
DMAIC can only be used in service processes, not in production
explanation: DMAIC is a structured project path for an existing process problem; PDCA is a repeating learning cycle. They are complementary rather than competing.

question: The purpose of a Gemba visit by leaders is to find who is to blame.
explanation: Leaders ask evidence-based questions, respect staff knowledge and avoid blame.

question: Which are the five Scrum values?
options: Commitment, Focus, Openness, Respect, Courage
Commitment, Speed, Openness, Respect, Courage
Focus, Quality, Trust, Respect, Courage
Planning, Focus, Openness, Respect, Humility
explanation: The three pillars are Transparency, Inspection and Adaptation.

question: Which are the three Scrum pillars?
options: Transparency, Planning, Adaptation
Transparency, Inspection, Adaptation
Commitment, Inspection, Delivery
Visibility, Feedback, Speed
explanation: The values are Commitment, Focus, Openness, Respect and Courage.
flag: The slide spells the third pillar "Adaption" (typo).

question: According to the Agile Manifesto, what is valued over comprehensive documentation?
options: Individuals and interactions
Customer collaboration
Working software
Responding to change
explanation: Individuals and interactions over processes and tools; working software over comprehensive documentation (the course slide words it "Working Product"); customer collaboration over contract negotiation; responding to change over following a plan.
flag: Image slide: read from the slide picture.

question: The Agile Manifesto says the items on the right (such as processes and tools) have no value.
explanation: "While there is value in the items on the right, we value the items on the left more."
flag: Image slide: read from the slide picture.

question: Agile/Scrum and waterfall are alternative definitions of Lean.
explanation: They are software delivery approaches, not definitions of Lean. They can coexist with Lean process improvement.

question: Which lists the five core elements of the ITIL 4 Service Value System?
options: Guiding principles, governance, service catalogue, incidents, continual improvement
Guiding principles, governance, service value chain, practices, continual improvement
Organizations & people, information & technology, partners & suppliers, value streams, practices
Plan, build, run, measure, improve
explanation: The second option lists the four dimensions.

question: Which is one of the four dimensions of ITIL 4?
options: Governance
Guiding principles
Partners & suppliers
Continual improvement
explanation: Dimensions: organizations & people; information & technology; partners & suppliers; value streams & processes. The other options are SVS elements.

question: How many service management practices does ITIL 4 list?
explanation: ITIL 4 lists 14 general management practices, 17 service management practices and 3 technical management practices.

question: Which is one of the four Kanban principles?
options: Limit work in progress
Maximize resource utilization
Increase batch size
Assign work by seniority
explanation: The four: visualise work, limit work in progress, focus on flow, continuous improvement.

question: Complete the four Kanban principles: Visualise work, ____ work in progress, Focus on flow, Continuous improvement.
explanation: Limit work in progress.

question: Which is the best definition of DevOps?
options: A project management method that replaces Scrum in software teams
A separate department that tests software before a release
Practices, culture and tools that unify development and operations
A framework for scaling agile across many teams and departments
explanation: Dev = development, Ops = IT operations. Full definition: a set of practices, a cultural philosophy and technical tools that unify software development and IT operations to deliver software more quickly, reliably and securely.

question: What does DevOps aim to shorten?
options: The time it takes to hire and train new developers
The length of each Scrum sprint in the team's planning
The time spent on writing documentation for a release
The time between committing a change and going live
explanation: DevOps aims to shorten the time between committing a system change and putting it into production, while ensuring high quality. It is a combination of technical practices, cultural changes and specific tools.

question: Which is NOT a key DevOps component?
options: Annual release planning
Culture and philosophy
Automation
Feedback loops
explanation: Key components: culture and philosophy, automation, continuous delivery, feedback loops.

question: CI/CD stands for continuous integration / continuous ____.
explanation: CI/CD stands for continuous integration / continuous deployment.

question: A team has many unfinished requests but few completed ones. Which Lean waste is most visible?
options: Overprocessing
Inventory
Motion
Defects
explanation: Many started but unfinished requests are work in progress piling up. That is Inventory waste: excess work in progress, stock or pending tickets. (Syllabus Ch.2, p.4)

question: A helpdesk measures time from ticket submission until the customer receives a solution, including queues. What is measured?
options: Cycle time at one station
Touch time
Takt time
Lead time
explanation: Lead time is the elapsed time from the customer's request to delivery, including waiting. Touch time counts only active work, takt time is the pace demand requires, and cycle time at a station covers one step. (Syllabus Ch.6, p.7)

question: Which statement best distinguishes Lean from Six Sigma?
options: Lean focuses on flow and waste; Six Sigma on variation and defects
Lean focuses only on factories; Six Sigma only on services
Lean measures quality; Six Sigma avoids data
Both methods focus exclusively on reducing staff
explanation: Lean asks where time and effort are wasted across the value stream. Six Sigma asks how reliably the process meets requirements. Neither is limited to manufacturing. (Syllabus Ch.1, p.3)

question: A team wants to discover whether repeated approvals cause delays. Which first step is most useful?
options: Buy new software
Set a higher output target
Map the current process and handoffs
Remove every approval immediately
explanation: Map the current state before designing a future state: a swimlane map makes handoffs and repeated approvals visible. Do not change things before you have seen the facts. (Syllabus Ch.5, p.6)

question: A customer says support should be fast. Which is the strongest CTQ?
options: Make support friendlier
Respond to 90% of priority tickets within 4 business hours
Hire more support staff
Reduce the number of support teams
explanation: A CTQ turns a broad need into something observable with a target and a unit. "Fast" becomes "90% of priority tickets get a response within 4 business hours". (Syllabus Ch.4, p.5)

question: Which example best illustrates Mura?
options: An agent works overtime daily
A form contains an error
A printer produces rejected pages
Requests arrive in large unpredictable batches
explanation: Mura is unevenness: irregular demand or workload. Daily overtime is Muri (overburden), and errors and rejected pages are Muda (waste, defects). (Syllabus Ch.1, p.3)

question: What is the main purpose of a SIPOC diagram?
options: Define high-level process boundaries and interfaces
Calculate statistical control limits
Identify each employee's daily tasks
Prove the root cause of a problem
explanation: A SIPOC sets the boundaries and interfaces of a process at a high level. It is not a detailed process map and it proves nothing. (Syllabus Ch.4, p.5)

question: In DMAIC, when should suspected root causes be tested against evidence?
options: Define
Control
Analyze
Improve
explanation: Analyze validates causes: suspected causes are tested against evidence, so a hypothesis becomes a verified root cause. (Syllabus Ch.3, p.5 and Ch.8, p.8)

question: A service team has 360 available minutes and demand of 120 requests per day. What is takt time?
options: 2 minutes per request
3 minutes per request
4 minutes per request
6 minutes per request
explanation: Takt time = available time ÷ demand = 360 ÷ 120 = 3 minutes per request. (Syllabus Ch.6, p.7)

question: A stable team has 60 open cases and completes 20 cases per day. What is average flow time under Little's Law?
options: 1 day
2 days
4 days
3 days
explanation: Little's Law: flow time = WIP ÷ throughput = 60 ÷ 20 = 3 days. (Syllabus Ch.6, p.7)

question: A team records 20 defects in 200 applications, with 2 defined defect opportunities per application. What is DPMO?
Which finding would best support a verified root cause?
options: A manager thinks the cause is training
The cause appears on a fishbone diagram
A controlled pilot addressing the cause reduces the problem
The cause was mentioned most often in a meeting
explanation: A root cause is verified when changing the cause changes the outcome, for example in a controlled pilot. Opinions, a fishbone and how often something is mentioned only give hypotheses. (Syllabus Ch.8, p.8)

question: What is a suitable use of a Pareto chart?
options: Measure the duration of each process step
Rank defect categories by their contribution
Document the five Lean principles
Calculate equipment availability
explanation: A Pareto chart ranks categories by frequency, cost or severity and shows the cumulative contribution. (Syllabus Ch.8, p.9)

question: A Kanban board has a limit of five tasks in progress. What is the main reason for this limit?
options: To eliminate the need for prioritization
To maximize the number of started tasks
To replace quality checks
To reduce overload and expose blocked work
explanation: Explicit WIP limits prevent overloading and make blocked work visible. (Syllabus Ch.10, p.10)

question: Which change is the best example of Poka Yoke?
options: A form prevents submission when a required field is empty
An annual meeting reviews mistakes
An employee is told to be more careful
A dashboard reports errors once per month
explanation: Poka Yoke is error-proofing: it makes errors hard to make or easy to spot, for example a required-format field that rejects invalid input. (Syllabus Ch.10, p.11)

question: Which 5S activity involves agreeing on consistent workplace routines?
options: Sort
Shine
Standardize
Set in Order
explanation: Standardize: agree visual standards and routines. Sort removes what is not needed, Set in Order locates and labels, Shine cleans and inspects. (Syllabus Ch.11, p.11)

question: A machine has 90% availability, 80% performance and 95% quality. What is its OEE?
explanation: OEE = Availability × Performance × Quality = 0.9 × 0.8 × 0.95 = 0.684 = 68.4%. (Syllabus Ch.12, p.12)

question: Why is a control plan needed after an improvement is implemented?
options: To avoid assigning process ownership
To restart the Define phase
To prove all future variation will disappear
To monitor performance and define responses to deterioration
explanation: A control plan keeps the improvement alive: clear owners, measures, thresholds and response rules. Variation never disappears. (Syllabus Ch.13, p.12)

question: Which conclusion about a fishbone diagram is correct?
options: It structures possible causes that still require verification
It statistically proves which cause is most important
It replaces process measurement
It is used only after implementing a solution
explanation: A fishbone organises hypotheses; it does not prove them. (Syllabus Ch.8, p.9)

question: A process has 10 minutes of value-added time and 100 minutes of total lead time. What is PCE?
explanation: PCE = value-added time ÷ total lead time × 100% = 10 ÷ 100 × 100 = 10%. (Syllabus Ch.5, p.6)

question: Scrum roles: who is accountable for maximizing the value of the product resulting from the work of the Scrum Team?
options: The Product Owner
The Scrum Master, who coaches the team
The Developers who build it
The stakeholders who pay for it
explanation: The Product Owner is accountable for maximizing the value of the product resulting from the work of the Scrum Team, and for managing the Product Backlog. (Scrum Guide 2020)

question: Scrum roles: what is the Scrum Master responsible for?
options: Deciding which items the team takes into the Sprint
Ensuring Scrum is understood and enacted
Ordering the items on the Product Backlog
Assigning tasks to each Developer
explanation: The Scrum Master is accountable for establishing Scrum as defined in the Scrum Guide, by helping everyone understand Scrum theory and practice, and for the effectiveness of the team. (Scrum Guide 2020)

question: Scrum events: what is the time-box for a Sprint?
options: Exactly 2 weeks
Between 1 and 3 months
1 month or less
Until the Product Backlog is empty
explanation: Sprints are fixed-length events of one month or less. A new Sprint starts right after the previous one ends. (Scrum Guide 2020)
flag: Scrum lecture 1 says "Sprint: 2 weeks to 1 month"; the Scrum Guide and the Kahoot say "one month or less". Both agree that a Sprint is never longer than one month.

question: Scrum events: which event is used to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the Sprint Backlog as necessary?
options: The Sprint Review
The Sprint Retrospective
Sprint Planning
The Daily Scrum
explanation: The purpose of the Daily Scrum is to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the Sprint Backlog as necessary. (Scrum Guide 2020)

question: Scrum artifacts: what does the Product Backlog contain?
options: An ordered list of everything that is needed in a product
Only the items that the Developers selected for the current Sprint, with their tasks
The tasks each Developer finished today
A fixed list of features agreed in a contract with the customer before the start
explanation: The Product Backlog is an emergent, ordered list of what is needed to improve the product. It is the single source of work for the Scrum Team. (Scrum Guide 2020)

question: Scrum artifacts: what is the purpose of the Definition of Done?
options: To list the tasks planned for the Sprint
To determine when a backlog item is complete
To describe the long-term goal of the product
To rank the backlog items by business value
explanation: The Definition of Done is a formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product. A backlog item that does not meet it is not done. (Scrum Guide 2020)
flag: The Kahoot answer reads "a print backlog item" (a typo for Sprint). In the Scrum Guide the Definition of Done applies to Product Backlog items, which become Sprint Backlog items once they are selected.

question: Scrum principles: what are the three pillars of Scrum?
options: Planning, Execution and Review of every Sprint
Commitment, Focus and Respect
Transparency, Inspection and Adaptation
Speed, Quality and Cost
explanation: Scrum rests on empiricism: Transparency enables Inspection, and Inspection without Adaptation is pointless. (Scrum Guide 2020)

question: Scrum principles: what is the purpose of the Sprint Retrospective?
options: To show the finished work to the stakeholders and collect their feedback
To plan the work for the next Sprint
To change the order of the Product Backlog
To inspect how the last Sprint went and plan improvements
explanation: The purpose of the Sprint Retrospective is to plan ways to increase quality and effectiveness. It concludes the Sprint. (Scrum Guide 2020)

question: Kanban principles: what is the first foundational principle of Kanban?
options: Visualize the workflow
Plan all the work up front
Maximize the utilization of every person
Fix the scope of each iteration
explanation: The Kanban Method starts by making the work visible: a board that shows the workflow.

question: Kanban principles: what does Kanban encourage regarding existing processes?
options: Replace them completely before you begin
Start with what you do now
Document them for a year first
Copy the process of a successful company
explanation: Kanban does not require a new process: you start with the current process and improve it step by step. (the Kanban Method's "start with what you do now")

question: Kanban principles: what is the purpose of limiting work in progress (WIP)?
options: To make sure everyone is busy all the time
To increase the number of tasks that are started
To improve flow and reduce bottlenecks
To reduce the number of quality checks
explanation: WIP limits prevent overload, make blocked work visible and keep work flowing. (Syllabus Ch.10, p.10)

question: Kanban practices: what does a Kanban board typically represent?
options: The yearly budget of the department and its spending
The organisation chart of the team
The release date of every feature
The workflow stages of the current work
explanation: A Kanban board shows the stages of the workflow as columns, with the work items moving across.

question: What is the goal of managing flow in Kanban?
options: To ensure work items move smoothly through the system
To make every item take exactly one week to finish in the system
To start as many items as possible
To keep everyone at 100% utilization
explanation: Managing flow means watching how work moves, removing blockers and queues, and keeping lead time predictable.

question: Which of the following is NOT a core Kanban practice?
options: Visualize the workflow on a board
Use time-boxed iterations
Limit work in progress
Make policies explicit
explanation: Time-boxed iterations (sprints) belong to Scrum. Kanban is continuous: visualise work, limit WIP, manage flow, make policies explicit, use feedback loops, improve together.

question: What is the primary goal of DevOps?
options: To replace the operations team with developers who also run production
To reduce the number of software releases
To improve collaboration between development and operations
To test the software only after it is released
explanation: DevOps unifies development and IT operations to deliver software faster, more reliably and more securely. (Scrum lecture 6)

question: Which of the following best describes the DevOps culture?
options: A strict separation of the duties of Dev and Ops
Finding the person to blame for each incident
One big release per year after long approvals
Shared responsibility and continuous learning
explanation: DevOps culture means shared responsibility for the product, collaboration across Dev and Ops, and learning from feedback.

question: What does CI/CD stand for in DevOps?
options: Continuous Integration / Continuous Deployment
Continuous Inspection / Continuous Documentation
Customer Interaction / Customer Delivery
Code Inspection / Code Distribution
explanation: CI/CD: continuous integration and continuous deployment (or delivery). Changes are integrated and released in small, automated steps. (Scrum lecture 6)

question: DevOps tools: which tool is commonly used for container orchestration?
options: Git and GitHub
Kubernetes
Selenium WebDriver
Jira Software
explanation: Kubernetes orchestrates containers. Git is version control, Selenium automates browser tests and Jira tracks work.

question: What is the role of monitoring in DevOps?
options: To approve each release by hand after a long checklist of sign-offs
To replace the automated tests
To observe system performance and detect issues early
To write down the requirements
explanation: Monitoring gives fast feedback on how the system behaves in production, so problems are found early.

question: What does "shift-left" mean in DevOps?
options: Moving all the testing to the period after the software has been released
Postponing security checks until production
Moving the team to another location
Performing tasks earlier in the development lifecycle
explanation: Shift-left means doing activities such as testing and security checks earlier, when problems are cheaper to fix.

question: ITIL 4 fundamentals: what is the purpose of the ITIL Service Value System (SVS)?
options: To deliver value through effective service management
To define the technical architecture of every system in detail
To measure the performance of each employee
To prescribe one fixed project plan
explanation: The Service Value System describes how all components and activities of an organisation work together to create value. (ITIL 4)

question: ITIL 4 fundamentals: which of the following is NOT one of the ITIL guiding principles?
options: Focus on value
Start from scratch
Keep it simple and practical
Collaborate and promote visibility
explanation: ITIL says "start where you are": use what already exists. "Start from scratch" is not a guiding principle. (ITIL 4)

question: Service value chain and practices: what is the central element of the Service Value System?
options: Governance of the organisation
The seven guiding principles
The service value chain
The continual improvement practice
explanation: The service value chain sits at the centre of the SVS: the operating model of activities that turn demand into value. (ITIL 4)

question: ITIL practices: what is the goal of the Continual Improvement practice?
options: To freeze the services as soon as they are live and stable
To reduce the number of services to one
To find the person to blame for incidents
To align services with changing business needs
explanation: Continual improvement aligns the organisation's practices and services with changing business needs through ongoing improvement. (ITIL 4)

question: Governance and culture: what role does governance play in the ITIL Service Value System?
options: It ensures alignment with the organisational objectives
It writes the code and tests for every single service in the portfolio
It replaces the service value chain
It hires the staff of the service desk
explanation: Governance directs and controls the organisation and keeps its activities aligned with its objectives. (ITIL 4)

question: Which ITIL 4 principle encourages experimentation and learning from failure?
options: Collaborate and promote visibility
Progress iteratively with feedback
Think and work holistically
Keep it simple and practical
explanation: Work in small steps, get feedback and adjust: that makes it safe to experiment and learn. (ITIL 4)

question: How big is a Scrum Team typically?
options: Exactly 7 people
Between 15 and 20 people
10 or fewer people
As many as the Product Owner can manage
explanation: A Scrum Team is a small unit of one Scrum Master, one Product Owner and Developers, typically 10 or fewer people. Larger groups split into several cohesive teams that share one Product Goal.

question: Which accountabilities make up a Scrum Team?
options: Project Manager, Product Owner and Testers
Scrum Master, Business Analyst and stakeholders
Product Owner, Team Lead and Developers
Scrum Master, Product Owner and Developers
explanation: A Scrum Team consists of one Scrum Master, one Product Owner and Developers. There are no sub-teams or hierarchies.

question: The Product Owner is one person, not a committee.
explanation: The Product Owner may represent the needs of many stakeholders, but is one person. The Product Owner can delegate work and remains accountable.

question: Who creates the Sprint Backlog?
options: The Developers
The Product Owner
The Scrum Master
The stakeholders
explanation: The Developers are accountable for creating the Sprint Backlog: the plan for the Sprint.

question: Who is accountable for instilling quality by following the Definition of Done?
options: The Product Owner
The Developers
The Scrum Master
The stakeholders
explanation: The Developers are accountable for instilling quality by adhering to the Definition of Done.

question: In Scrum, the Scrum Master decides who does what in the team.
explanation: A Scrum Team is self-managing: its members decide internally who does what, when and how. The Scrum Master serves the team, coaching self-management.

question: What does empiricism mean in Scrum?
options: Knowledge comes from a detailed plan that is made and approved before the work starts
Knowledge comes from the opinion of the most senior person
Knowledge comes from experience and from decisions based on what is observed
Knowledge comes from following the rules exactly as written
explanation: Scrum is founded on empiricism (and lean thinking): you learn by doing, observing and adapting.

question: What does transparency mean in Scrum?
options: Only the Product Owner may see the Sprint Backlog and the work in progress of the team
Team members report their hours to management every week
Stakeholders may not look at work in progress
The work and the process are visible to those who do the work and those who receive it
explanation: Transparency enables inspection. Inspection without transparency is misleading and wasteful.

question: Inspection without adaptation is pointless.
explanation: Scrum events provide cadence for inspection, and the team is expected to adapt the moment it learns something new.

question: How long is the Daily Scrum?
options: 15 minutes
30 minutes
1 hour
As long as the Developers need
explanation: The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute event for the Developers, held at the same time and place every working day.

question: The Daily Scrum is an event for the Developers of the Scrum Team.
explanation: It is a 15-minute event for the Developers. The Product Owner and Scrum Master take part only when they are working on items of the Sprint Backlog.

question: Which three questions does Sprint Planning address?
options: What was built, who liked it and what is next
Why is this Sprint valuable, what can be done and how will the chosen work get done
What went well, what went wrong and what to improve
Who is on the team, how long does the project last, what does it cost and who signs it off
explanation: Sprint Planning: topic one (why: the Sprint Goal), topic two (what: the Product Backlog items), topic three (how: the plan to deliver them).

question: What is the maximum time-box of Sprint Planning for a one-month Sprint?
options: 2 hours
4 hours
8 hours
16 hours
explanation: Sprint Planning is time-boxed to a maximum of eight hours for a one-month Sprint; for shorter Sprints it is usually shorter.

question: What is the maximum time-box of the Sprint Review for a one-month Sprint?
options: 1 hour
8 hours
2 days
4 hours
explanation: The Sprint Review is time-boxed to a maximum of four hours for a one-month Sprint.

question: What is the maximum time-box of the Sprint Retrospective for a one-month Sprint?
options: 3 hours
30 minutes
6 hours
1 day
explanation: The Sprint Retrospective is time-boxed to a maximum of three hours for a one-month Sprint.

question: What is the purpose of the Sprint Review?
options: To plan how the team will improve its way of working during the next Sprint and beyond
To inspect the outcome of the Sprint with the stakeholders and decide what to adapt
To decide which Developer worked hardest
To plan the tasks for the next 24 hours
explanation: The Sprint Review inspects the outcome of the Sprint and determines future adaptations. The team presents results to key stakeholders and discusses progress toward the Product Goal.

question: The Sprint Review is nothing more than a presentation to the stakeholders.
explanation: The Sprint Review is a working session. The Scrum Team should avoid limiting it to a presentation.

question: Which event concludes the Sprint?
options: The Sprint Review with the stakeholders
The Daily Scrum
The Sprint Retrospective
Sprint Planning
explanation: The Sprint Retrospective concludes the Sprint. It comes after the Sprint Review.

question: Who can cancel a Sprint?
options: The Scrum Master, when the team falls behind
The Developers, when the work turns out to be harder than they expected at planning
Any stakeholder who wants to change the scope
Only the Product Owner, if the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete
explanation: A Sprint could be cancelled if the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete. Only the Product Owner has the authority to cancel the Sprint.

question: A new Sprint starts immediately after the previous Sprint ends.
explanation: Sprints are fixed-length events of one month or less, and a new Sprint starts right after the previous one.

question: What is the Sprint?
options: A fixed-length event of one month or less that contains all the other events
A planning meeting held once per quarter, in which the roadmap of the year is decided
A phase in which only testing is done
The meeting where the stakeholders accept the product
explanation: The Sprint is the heartbeat of Scrum: the container for all other events, where ideas are turned into value.

question: Which artifact and commitment belong together?
options: Product Backlog and the Sprint Goal of the team
Increment and the Definition of Done
Sprint Backlog and the Product Goal
Increment and the Product Goal
explanation: Product Backlog: Product Goal. Sprint Backlog: Sprint Goal. Increment: Definition of Done.

question: What is the Product Goal?
options: The single objective of one Sprint
The checklist an Increment must meet
The long-term objective of the Scrum Team
The plan for delivering the selected items
explanation: The Product Goal describes a future state of the product and is the commitment of the Product Backlog. The team fulfils it or abandons it before it takes on the next one.

question: What is the Sprint Goal?
options: The long-term objective of the product
The list of everything the product needs
The quality standard of the Increment
The single objective for the Sprint
explanation: The Sprint Goal is the commitment of the Sprint Backlog. It is created during Sprint Planning and gives the Developers flexibility in the work.

question: What does the Sprint Backlog consist of?
options: The Sprint Goal (why), the selected Product Backlog items (what) and a plan to deliver them (how)
All the Product Backlog items, ordered by value, with the estimated effort per item and the release dates
Only the tasks that are already finished
The Definition of Done and the release dates
explanation: The Sprint Backlog is a plan by and for the Developers: why, what and how. It is updated throughout the Sprint.

question: Work that does not meet the Definition of Done can still be shown at the Sprint Review.
explanation: Work that does not meet the Definition of Done cannot be part of the Increment, released or presented at the Sprint Review. It goes back to the Product Backlog.

question: When is an Increment born?
options: When the Sprint Review has ended and the stakeholders have given feedback
When a Product Backlog item meets the Definition of Done
When the Product Owner writes the item down
When the Developers start working on the item
explanation: The moment a Product Backlog item meets the Definition of Done, an Increment is born.

question: The Product Backlog is a fixed list that is complete before the first Sprint starts.
explanation: The Product Backlog is emergent: an ordered list that is continually refined as the team learns.

question: Which statement describes the waterfall model?
options: An approach with short iterations that each deliver a potentially shippable product to the customer
A method in which all phases run in parallel with daily meetings
A linear, sequential approach in which one phase must be finished before the next begins
A framework in which the customer re-orders the work every day
explanation: Waterfall has distinct, sequential phases, like a waterfall flowing downwards. Scrum works in short time-boxed iterations instead.

question: Which description of Agile is correct?
options: A strict approach in which each phase is signed off in full by management before the next phase can begin
A set of tools for automating software deployment
A checklist of best practices for managing IT services
A flexible, collaborative approach with continuous improvement that delivers value in iterations
explanation: Agile is a project management and software development approach focused on flexibility, collaboration and continuous improvement, delivering value iteratively. The last option describes ITIL.

question: Which of these is NOT part of the Agile family?
options: ITIL
Scrum
Kanban
DevOps
explanation: ITIL is not part of the Agile family: it is a framework of best practices for managing IT services.

question: How do ITIL and Lean differ?
options: ITIL emphasizes speed; Lean emphasizes stability, documentation and fixed procedures for every service
ITIL emphasizes processes and stability; Lean emphasizes speed and continuous improvement
ITIL is a Lean tool for waste reduction; Lean is a service catalogue
Both apply only to software development teams
explanation: ITIL provides a structured framework for managing IT services over their lifecycle; Lean focuses on eliminating waste and maximising value for the customer.

question: Which of these is a characteristic of Scrum?
options: A prescribed set of engineering practices
A project manager who assigns the tasks
Self-organizing teams
A fixed plan for the whole project
explanation: Scrum characteristics: self-organizing teams, working with the customer, month-long sprints, requirements as items in a product backlog, no specific engineering practices prescribed.

question: In Scrum, how are requirements captured?
options: In a contract fixed before the project starts
In a detailed specification written by the Scrum Master
As tickets in a service catalogue
As items in a list called the product backlog
explanation: Requirements are captured as items in a "product backlog".

question: Scrum prescribes specific engineering practices.
explanation: Scrum prescribes none: it is a framework of roles, events and artifacts, and uses generative rules to create an agile environment.

question: Which five factors explain why products get more complex every day?
options: Scale, diversity, connectivity, dynamics, refinement
Speed, quality, cost, scope, risk, time and resources
Plan, do, check, act, standardize, sustain and improve
Value, flow, pull, perfection, waste
explanation: Products are getting more complex every day because of scale, diversity, connectivity, dynamics and refinement.

question: Which statement compares Scrum and waterfall correctly?
options: Scrum finishes every phase for the whole product before the next phase can start, like a waterfall
Scrum works in short time-boxed iterations and aims at a potentially shippable product
Scrum delivers the product once, at the end of the project
Scrum has no planning at all
explanation: Scrum: short time-boxed iterations (a Sprint is "2 weeks to 1 month" in some material and "one month or less" in the Scrum Guide); developers focus on a potentially shippable product.

question: Which is one of the core practices of the Kanban Method?
options: Assign story points to every item
Hold a Sprint Review after each iteration
Make policies explicit
Use fixed-length iterations
explanation: The Kanban Method's practices: visualise the workflow, limit work in progress, manage flow, make policies explicit, implement feedback loops, improve collaboratively and evolve experimentally.

question: Which is one of the seven ITIL 4 guiding principles?
options: Start from scratch
Work in silos
Keep it complex and thorough
Start where you are
explanation: The seven guiding principles: focus on value; start where you are; progress iteratively with feedback; collaborate and promote visibility; think and work holistically; keep it simple and practical; optimize and automate.

question: Which six activities form the ITIL 4 service value chain?
options: Plan, improve, engage, design and transition, obtain/build, deliver and support
Define, measure, analyze, improve and control, followed by a report to the sponsor at the end
Plan, do, check, act, standardize, sustain
Sort, set in order, shine, standardize, sustain, safety
explanation: The service value chain turns demand into value through six activities: plan, improve, engage, design and transition, obtain/build, deliver and support. The wrong options are PDCA, DMAIC and 5S.

question: Available production time is 27,600 seconds per day and customer demand is 460 pieces per day. What is the takt time?
options: 46 seconds
60 seconds
120 seconds
600 seconds
explanation: Takt time = available production time per day ÷ customer demand per day = 27,600 ÷ 460 = 60 seconds.

question: Which definition describes production lead time?
options: How often a part or product is actually completed by a process, as timed by an observer with a stopwatch
The required pace to meet customer demand
The time it takes one piece to move all the way through a process or value stream, from start to finish
The time an operator needs for one work element
explanation: Production lead time is the time one piece needs from beginning to end of the value stream. Cycle time is how often a piece is completed, as timed by observation.
src: Cycle time and lead time slide

question: Which definition describes cycle time (CT)?
options: The time one piece needs to travel through the whole value stream, from the first step to the last step
The required pace to meet customer demand
The time between a customer request and delivery
How often a part or product is actually completed by a process, as timed by observation
explanation: Cycle time: how often a part or product is completed by a process, as timed by observation; also the time an operator needs to go through all work elements before repeating them.
src: Cycle time and lead time slide

question: How should the problem be described in a project charter?
options: In clear, coherent terms: how often, where and who is bothered (5xW, 1xH)
Only with the expected financial benefit of the project, summed over the first three years
Together with the preferred solution
As a single sentence that names who is to blame
explanation: Problem description: describe the problem in clear, coherent terms (5xW 1xH): how often does it occur, where does it take place, who is bothered by it. Do not add a preferred solution.

question: Which Lean Six Sigma role is the executive leader who drives the initiative?
options: The Master Black Belt
The Champion
The Black Belt
The Green Belt
explanation: Champion: executive leader who drives the initiative, helps select projects and remove barriers for project teams, and supports change and the Lean Six Sigma culture.

question: How does Lean Six Sigma relate to Lean and Six Sigma?
options: Lean replaces Six Sigma, because removing waste automatically removes defects as well
Six Sigma replaces Lean, because statistics are more reliable than process improvement
Lean (waste) plus Six Sigma (defects) in one approach: Lean strengthens Six Sigma
Two rival approaches that cannot be combined within one organisation
explanation: Lean focuses on waste reduction by streamlining a process. Six Sigma focuses on preventing defects through problem solving. Together: problem solving plus improving processes delivers greater results.
src: Six Sigma vs Lean Six Sigma slide

question: Hout enzo B.V. has a customer demand of 15,000 finished products per year, 250 working days and 450 available minutes per day. What is the takt time (minutes per product)?
explanation: 15,000 ÷ 250 = 60 products per day. Takt time = 450 ÷ 60 = 7.5 minutes per product.

question: In the Hout enzo process the step "Assembling" has an opening stock of 95, an inflow of 25 and a closing stock of 65. What is its output in the period?
explanation: Output per step = opening stock + inflow − closing stock = 95 + 25 − 65 = 55.

question: The Assembling step of Hout enzo has an output of 55 products in a 450-minute day. What is its average cycle time (minutes per product, 2 decimals)?
explanation: Average cycle time = 450 ÷ output = 450 ÷ 55 = 8.18 minutes per product.

question: Takt time is 7.50 minutes. Cycle times are: Sort material 5.29, Assembling 8.18, Apply lacquer layer 7.50, Packing and sending 6.92 minutes. Which step does not meet the takt time?
options: Sort material
Apply lacquer layer
Packing and sending
Assembling
explanation: Only Assembling has a cycle time above takt (8.18 > 7.50), so it is the capacity bottleneck. Apply lacquer layer equals the takt time exactly.

question: What does it mean when the cycle time of a step is greater than the takt time?
options: The step cannot keep pace with customer demand, so backlogs and delivery delays may arise
The step is faster than the takt time requires and therefore always has idle capacity left
The step produces too many defects
The step is not part of the value stream
explanation: A cycle time above takt means the step cannot sustainably keep pace with demand at the measured output rate.

question: Hout enzo: total processing time is 58.58 minutes and the total lead time is 3,377.71 minutes. What is the process efficiency (percentage, 2 decimals)?
explanation: Process efficiency = total processing time ÷ total lead time × 100 = 58.58 ÷ 3,377.71 × 100 = 1.73%.

question: Which set of measures best improves the process efficiency of the Hout enzo line?
options: Add more inspection steps after Assembling, so that every defect is found before the products are packed
Reduce inventories and waiting, balance the steps, fix the Assembling bottleneck and move towards pull
Increase the batch sizes between steps so that every step can keep working
Let every step work as fast as it can, whatever the demand
